<!-- theoreme-1: body_md -->
$\mathrm{(Luo, Theorem 1.5)}$

A hyperbolic component $\mathcal{H}$ admits bounded escape if and only if it has nested Julia sets.
<!-- end theoreme-1 -->
<!-- theoreme-2: body_md -->
$\mathrm{(Ma\tilde{n}\acute e -Sad-Sullivan)}$

Let $X$ be a complex connected manifold and $f : X\times \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \rightarrow X\times \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ be a holomorphic family of rational maps parametrized by $X$. For $\lambda \in X$, let us denote $f_\lambda : \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ the associated rational map.

Let $x\in X$. Then the following conditions are equivalent :
\begin{enumerate}
\item The number of attracting cycles of $f_\lambda$ is locally constant at $x$.
\item The maximum period of an attracting cycle of $f_\lambda$ is locally bounded at $x$. 
\item The Julia set moves holomorphically at $x$. 
\item For all $y$ sufficiently close to $x$, every periodic point of $f_y$ is attracting, repelling or persistently indifferent.
\item The Julia set depends continuously on $\lambda$ (in the analytic topology) on a neighborhood of $x$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theoreme-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
(infra theorem \ref{JuliaSetMovesContinuouslyNonArchi})

Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space with no boundary. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps and $x \in X$. Let us assume that $f_x$ has type I repelling points. Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
    \item The Julia set depends continously on $\lambda$ on a neighborhood of $x$, 
    \item For all $y$ sufficiently close to $x$, every point of $f_y$ is attracting, repelling or persistently indifferent. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
(infra propositon \ref{JuliaSetsMovesContinuouslyIfAttractingBounded})

Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space with no boundary. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps of degree $d \geq 2$. Let us assume that $\mathrm{char}(\tilde{k}) = 0$ or $\mathrm{char}(\tilde{k}) = p >d$. Let $x\in X$ such that $f_x$ has type I repelling points. 

Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The Julia set depends continously on $\lambda$ on a neighborhood of $x$, 
    \item The number of attracting cycles is constant on a neighborhood of $x$,
    \item The maximum period of an attracting cycle of $f_\lambda$ is locally bounded at $x$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
(infra theorem \ref{Julia set moves continuously hybrid setting})

Let $\mathbb{C}$ be equipped with the hybrid norm and $X$ a flowing $\mathbb{C}_{hyb}$-analytic space. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps and $x \in X$. 

\begin{itemize}
\item If $x \in X_{>0}$, then the Julia set moves continuously on a flowing neighborhood of $x$ if and only if it moves continuously on a neighborhood $U_{\mathrm{pr}(x)}$ of $x$ seen in the fiber $X_{\mathrm{pr}(x)}$,

\item If $x\in X_0$, then the Julia set moves continuously on a flowing neighborhood of $x$ if and only if there is a flowing neighborhood $U$ of $f_x$ such that :
\begin{enumerate}
\item the Julia sets moves continuously on $U_{>0}$,
\item for all $y\in U_0$, every indifferent point of $f_y$ is hybridly persistently non-repelling.
\end{enumerate} 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
(infra theorem \ref{InGoodHyperbolicComponentsJuliaSetContinuousIFFMulitpliersBlowUp})

Let $U$ be a hyperbolic connected component of $\mathrm{M}_d(\mathbb{C})$ such that the Julia sets do not have indifferent periodic point. Let $\tilde{f}_i$ be a degenerating net in $U$.

Then the Julia set of $\tilde{f}_i$ degenerates continuously if and only if all of the multipliers of its repelling points blow-up.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
Let us denote $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}$ the affine space of dimension $n$ over $A$.

The underlying space is the set of all bounded multiplicative semi-norms over $A[T_1, \cdots, T_n]$. Hence, it is the set of applications :
\begin{equation*}
|\cdot| : A[T_1, \cdots, T_n] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
\end{equation*}
such that :
\begin{itemize}
\item $|0| = 0$ and $|1| = 1$,
\item $\forall P,Q \in A[T_1, \cdots, T_n], |PQ| = |P| |Q|$,
\item $\forall P,Q \in A[T_1, \cdots, T_n], |P + Q| \leq |P| + |Q|$,
\item $\forall a\in A, |a| \leq \vert\vert a \vert\vert.$
\end{itemize}

We denote by $\mathcal{M}(A)$ the space $\mathbf{A}^{0,an}_A$ and call it the Berkovich spectrum of $A$. We have a projection $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A \rightarrow \mathcal{M}(A)$ induced by the injection $A \hookrightarrow A[T_1, \cdots, T_n]$.

If $x \in \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A$, we denote $|\cdot|_x$ the associated semi-norm. The ring $A[T_1, \cdots, T_n]/(ker~|\cdot|_x)$ is an integral domain, so we may look at its fraction field. As $|\cdot|_x$ is inducing an absolute value on it, we may take its completion and we denote it $\mathcal{H}(x).$

There is a topology on $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A$. Let us take the coarsest topology such that for all $P \in A[T_1, \cdots, T_n]$, the applications
\begin{center}
$\begin{cases}
\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A &\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},\\
|\cdot|_x &\mapsto |P|_x
\end{cases}
$
\end{center}
are continuous. With this topology, $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A$ is Hausdorff and locally compact. Furthermore, $\mathcal{M}(A)$ is compact. The projection $\mathrm{pr} : \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_A \rightarrow \mathcal{M}(A)$ is continuous.
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
An example of a Banach ring we will use is the hybrid field. Let $(k,|\cdot|)$ be non-trivially valued field, then we define on $k$ a hybrid norm $|\cdot|_{hyb}$ such that
\begin{center}
$|x|_{hyb} = \max(|x|, |x|_{trivial})$.
\end{center}
It gives a Banach ring.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
If $X$ is a scheme of locally finite presentation over $A$ where $A$ is a geometric base ring, which includes valued and hybrid fields, then we may consider its analytification. It is a $A$-analytic space in the sense of Berkovich which we denote by $X^{an}$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
For a precise definition of geometric base ring, we may refer for example to the book of T. Lemanissier - J. Poineau (\cite{LemanissierPoineau}, Définition 3.3.8).
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
If $X$ and $Y$ are two $A$-schemes locally of finite presentation and $f : X \rightarrow Y$ a scheme morphism, then we can consider its analytification $f$ to get $f^{an} : X^{an} \rightarrow Y^{an}$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{morphisme fini sur meme dimension est ouvert} Lemma 3.2.4 of \cite{BerkovichLivre}

Let $\phi : X \rightarrow Y$ a finite morphsim of $k$-analytic spaces such that $\dim(X) = \dim(Y)$ and $X$ is locally irreducible. Then $\phi$ is an open morphism.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- rem-2: body_md -->
The fact that the morphsim has finite fibers is enough see for example Théorème 5.2.9 of \cite{LemanissierPoineau}.
<!-- end rem-2 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
Let $(k, |\cdot|)$ be a valued field and let us denote $k_{hyb}$ the field equipped with the hybrid  norm. Then, the Berkovich spectrum is :
\begin{center}
$\mathcal{M}(k_{hyb}) = [0,1]$,
\end{center} 
where the identification comes from the association to any $0\leq \varepsilon \leq 1$ to the absolute value $|\cdot|^\varepsilon$, $|\cdot|^0$ is the trivial absolute value.

Hence, the residue fields $\mathcal{H}(\varepsilon)$ are the completion of $k$ equipped with the absolue value $|\cdot|^\varepsilon$. Let us denote them $\hat{k}_\varepsilon$.   

A $k_{hyb}$-analytic space $X$ is equipped with a projection $\mathrm{pr} : X \rightarrow \mathcal{M}(k_{hyb})$. 

For all $\varepsilon \in [0,1], \mathrm{pr}^{-1}(\varepsilon) =: X_\varepsilon$ is a $\mathcal{H}(\varepsilon)$-analytic space.
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- rem-3: body_md -->
If $X$ is a $k_{hyb}$-analytic space, where $k$ is a complete field, for all $\varepsilon > 0, X_\varepsilon$ have isomorphic underlying topologic spaces: all the spaces $\mathcal{H}(\varepsilon)$-analytic spaces are $k$-analytics spaces equipped with a different normalisation. And for $\varepsilon = 0, X_0$ is an analytic space over a trivially valued field.

In the case, where $k$ is an archimedean field, then for $\epsilon > 0$, one has complex analytic spaces and for $\varepsilon = 0$ one finds a Berkovich space of non-archimedean nature. 

Hence, the hybrid fields can link archimedean and non-archimedean phenomena.
<!-- end rem-3 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
Let $\varepsilon \in [0,1]$, then we define :
\begin{center}
$I_\varepsilon :=
		\begin{cases}
        [0, +\infty[ & \mathrm{if}~ \varepsilon = 0\\
        [0, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}] & \mathrm{else.}    
        \end{cases}$
\end{center}
Let us denote $I^*_\varepsilon := I_\varepsilon \backslash \lbrace 0 \rbrace$.

Furthermore, if $S$ is a $k_{hyb}$-analytic space, then with the projection $\mathrm{pr} : S \rightarrow \mathcal{M}(k_{hyb})$, for all $x\in S$, we define $I_x := I_{\mathrm{pr}(x)}$.
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
Let $x \in \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$ and $\alpha \in I_x$, then the application :
\begin{center}
$P \in k[T_1, \cdots, T_n] \mapsto |P(x)|^\alpha \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ 
\end{center}
defines a point of $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$ which we denote by $x^\alpha$. We have $\mathrm{pr}(x^\alpha) = \alpha ~ \mathrm{pr}(x)$.

Furthermore, if $\alpha \in I^*_x$, then the fields $\mathcal{H}(x)$ and $\mathcal{H}(x^\alpha)$ are isomorphic.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
Let 
\begin{center}
$D(\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}) := \bigcup_{x \in \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}} \lbrace x\rbrace \times I_x^\alpha \subset \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}} \times \mathbb{R}_{> 0}$.
\end{center}
Then the flow is the application :
\begin{center}
$\Phi : \begin{cases} 
		D(\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}) &\rightarrow \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}},\\
		(x,\alpha)&\mapsto x^\alpha.
		\end{cases}$
\end{center}
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
The flow is a continuous and open application.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
Let $x \in \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$, then the trajectory of the point $x$ is the set $T(x)$ defined by :
\begin{center}
$T(x) := \Phi(x, I_x^*) = \lbrace x^\alpha, \alpha \in I_x^*\rbrace.$ 
\end{center}
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- rem-4: body_md -->
Let $x, y\in \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$. If $y \in T(x)$ then $T(y) = T(x)$.
<!-- end rem-4 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
\label{def trajectoire ensemble}
Let $V$ be a subset of $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$, then the trajectory of $V$ is the set
\begin{center}
$T(V) := \bigcup_{x\in V} T(x) \subset \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$.
\end{center}

If $V = T(V)$, then $V$ will be said to be flowing. 

Furthermore, if $V, V'$ are two subsets of $\mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$, then $T(V\cup V') = T(V) \cup T(V')$ and $T(V\cap V') = T(V) \cap T(V')$.
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- defi-6: body_md -->
\label{flowing k hyb -analytic space}
A flowing local $k_{hyb}$-analytic model is the data of an integer $n$, a flowing open $U \subset \mathbf{A}^{n,an}_{k_{hyb}}$ and a closed analytic subset of $U$.

A flowing $k_{hyb}$-analytic space is a $k_{hyb}$-analytic space obtained by gluing flowing local $k_{hyb}$-analytic models along flowing open subsets.
<!-- end defi-6 -->
<!-- defi-7: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $k$-variety, then let us define
\begin{center}
$X_\infty := X^{an}_0 \backslash X^\beth$
\end{center}
it is an open of $X^{an}_0$. Hence, it is a $k_0$-analytic space.
<!-- end defi-7 -->
<!-- ex-2: body_md -->
\label{exemple de X infty}
If $X = \mathbf{A}^1_k$, let us denote $\eta_{a,r} \in \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_{k_0}$ the semi-norm $P = \sum a_k(T-a)^k \mapsto \mathrm{max}|a_k|_0 r^k$. As $k_0$ is trivially valued, $\eta_{a,r} \leq 1 \iff \eta_{a,r}(T-a) \leq 1 \iff \eta_{a,r}(T) \leq 1 \iff r\leq 1$. Hence,

\begin{center}
$(\mathbf{A}^1_k)_\infty = \lbrace x\in \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_{k_0}, \exists P\in k[T] |P(x)| >1\rbrace = \lbrace \eta_{0,r}, r\in \mathbb{R}_{>1}\rbrace$.
\end{center}

Equally, if $X = \mathbf{G}_{m,k}$ then

\begin{align*}
(\mathbb{G}_{m,k})_\infty &= \lbrace x\in \mathbb{G}^{an}_{m,k_0}, \exists P\in k[T, T^{-1}] |P(x)| >1\rbrace \\
&= \lbrace x\in \mathbb{G}^{an}_{m,k_0}, \mathrm{max} (|T(x)|, |T^{-1}(x)|) >1\rbrace \\
&= \lbrace \eta_{0,r}, r\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}, r\neq 1\rbrace.
\end{align*}
<!-- end ex-2 -->
<!-- defi-8: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $k$ variety, then we define
\begin{center}
$X^+ := X^{hyb} \backslash X^\beth$.
\end{center}
It is an open of $X^{hyb}$ and so it is a $k_{hyb}$-analytic space. One may remark that $X^+_0 = X_\infty$.
<!-- end defi-8 -->
<!-- prop-5: body_md -->
Let $X, Y$ be two $k$-varieties and $f : X \rightarrow Y$ a proper morphism. Then the analytification $f^{hyb} : X^{hyb} \rightarrow Y^{hyb}$ is proper and restricts to a morphism $f^+ : X^+ \rightarrow Y^+$.
<!-- end prop-5 -->
<!-- defi-9: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $k$-variety and let $x,y \in X^{hyb}$. We say that $x,y$ are equivalent through the flow if $T(x) = T(y)$ and we denote it $x \Phi y$.
<!-- end defi-9 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $k$-variety, then $\Phi$ is an equivalence relation.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- defi-10: body_md -->
\label{immersion de Xan dans compactification}
Let $X$ be a $k$-variety, the set
\begin{center}
$X^\urcorner := X^+/\Phi$
\end{center}
is called the valuative compactification of $X$ or hybrid compactification. We equip this set with the quotient topology, so in particular the image of a subset $V$ of $X^+$ is open if and only if $T(V)$ is open in $X^+$.

Let us denote $q : X^+ \rightarrow X^\urcorner$ the quotient application. 

Let us denote $\delta X := q(X_\infty)$ the boundary of the compactification.

Finally, let us denote $i$ the following immersion:
\begin{center}
$i : (X \otimes_k \hat{k})^{an} = X_1^+ \rightarrow X^+ \rightarrow X^\urcorner$,
\end{center} 
where $\hat{k}$ is the completion of $k$.
<!-- end defi-10 -->
<!-- prop-6: body_md -->
\label{prop section continue partie archi} Lemma 4.11 and 4.15 of \cite{PoineauCompactificationHybride}.

Let $k$ be a field equipped with a non trivial absolute value. Let $X$ be a $k$ variety, then we may consider its analytification $X^{an}$ with respect to this norm on $k$.

And $i : X^{an} \rightarrow X^\urcorner$ is an homeomorphism into its image.
<!-- end prop-6 -->
<!-- ex-3: body_md -->
We saw at the example \ref{exemple de X infty} that $(\mathbf{A}^1_k)_\infty = \lbrace \eta_{0,r}, r>1\rbrace$, so $\delta (\mathbf{A}^1_k)$ is a unique point. And $(\mathbb{G}_{m,k})_\infty = \lbrace \eta_{0,r}, r>0, r\neq 1\rbrace$, so $\delta (\mathbb{G}_{m,k})$ is two points.
<!-- end ex-3 -->
<!-- prop-7: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a $k$-variety. Then, $X^\urcorner$ is Hausdorff and compact. Furthermore, $X^{an}$ is dense in $X^\urcorner$. 

Furthermore, $X^\urcorner$ is locally path-connected and if $X$ is connected, $X^\urcorner$ is path-connected.

If $k$ is countable, then $X^\urcorner$ is metrizable.
<!-- end prop-7 -->
<!-- defi-11: body_md -->
Let $G$ be an abelian group, we write it multiplicatively. A $G$ graded ring is a ring $A$ with a unity $1$ 
\begin{center}
$A = \bigoplus_{g\in G} A_g$
\end{center}
such that $A_hA_g \subset A_{gh}$ and $1 \in A_1$. 

A homomorphism of $G$ graded ring is a homomorphism $\phi : A\rightarrow B$ such that $\phi(A_g) \subset B_g, \forall g\in G$.

A graded field is a graded ring with no non-zero homogeneous ideals. It is equivalent to the condition that all non-zero homogeneous element of $A$ are invertible. 

A graded ring $A$ is called local graded ring if it has a unique maximal homogeneous ideal $m$. 

Let $K$ be a graded field. We say that a graded subring $A\subset K$ is a graded valuation ring if it is a local graded ring whose quotient field is $K$ and for any non-zero homogeneous $f\in K$, at least one of the two elements $f, f^{-1}$ belongs to $A$. Any local graded ring $B\subset K$ is dominated by a graded valuation subring of $K$. 

Let $k\subset K$ be two graded fields. We denote by $\mathbb{P}_{K/k} = \mathbb{P}_K$ the set of all graded valuation rings $\mathcal{O}$ such that $k\subset \mathcal{O}$ and the quotient field of $\mathcal{O}$ is $K$. One endows $\mathbb{P}_K$ with the weakest topology with respect to which the set $\lbrace \mathcal{O}\in \mathbb{P}_K, f\in \mathcal{O}\rbrace$ is open for any homogeneous element $f\in K$.

Given $X\subset \mathbb{P}_K$ and $A\subset K$, we define $X\lbrace A\rbrace = \lbrace \mathcal{O}\in \mathbb{P}_K, f\in \mathcal{O}$ for all homogeneous $f\in A\rbrace$.
<!-- end defi-11 -->
<!-- defi-12: body_md -->
Let $B$ be a Banach $k$-algebra. Let us denote by $\rho_B$ the spectral semi-norm of $B$. Then, for all positive real number $r$, we set $B_r^\circ = \lbrace x\in B, \rho_B(x)\leq r\rbrace, B_r^{\circ\circ} = \lbrace x\in B, \rho_B(x) < r\rbrace$ and $\tilde{B}_r = B_r^\circ/B_r^{\circ\circ}$.

Let 
\begin{center}
$\tilde{B} = \bigoplus_{r>0} \tilde{B}_r$.
\end{center}
We call it the reduction ring of $B$. 

Any bounded homomorphism $B \rightarrow D$ of Banach $k$-algebras induces a homomorphism $\tilde{B} \rightarrow \tilde{D}$ of $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ graded $\tilde{k}$-algebras.
<!-- end defi-12 -->
<!-- defi-13: body_md -->
\label{Definition chi_x}
The germ corresponding to a punctural $k$-analytic space $(X,x)$ is denoted $X_x$. A germ is called good if the point $x$ admits an affinoid neighborhood in $X$. 

Let $(Y,x)$ be a punctural $k$-analytic space such that the germ is good. Let $X= M(A)$ be an affinoid neighborhood of $x$, we have a bounded morphism $\chi_x : A \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x)$, and we set 
\begin{center}
$\widetilde{X_x} = \mathbb{P}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}}(\widetilde{\chi_x}(\tilde{A}))$.
\end{center}
It does not depend on the choice of the neighborhood $X$. 

If $f = (f_1, \cdots, f_n) \in \mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ and $r = (r_1, \cdots, r_n) \in \mathbb{R}^*_+$, then we define $X_x\lbrace r_i^{-1}f_i\rbrace$ as the germ corresponding to the punctured space $(Z,x)$ with $Z = \lbrace y \in X, |f_i(y)| \leq r_i\rbrace$.
<!-- end defi-13 -->
<!-- rem-5: body_md -->
Temkin actually defines the reduction of germs for all germs, but we only need the definition in this case.
<!-- end rem-5 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma Temkin}
Given a good germ $X_x$ and a family $f = (f_1, \cdots, f_n)\subset \mathcal{O}_{X,x}$, one has $\widetilde{X_x\lbrace r_i^{-1}f_i\rbrace} = \widetilde{X_x}\lbrace \tilde{f_i}\rbrace$ where $r_i = |f_i(x)|$ and $\tilde{f_i}$ is the image of $f_i$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}$.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- defi-14: body_md -->
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean value field and $X = M(\mathcal{A})$ be a $k$-affinoid space. To every point $x\in  X$, one has an associated bounded $k$-homomorphism $\chi_x : \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x)$ as in definition \ref{Definition chi_x}. It is called inner if there is a admissible epimorphism $\pi : k\lbrace r_1^{-1}T_1, \cdots, r_n^{-1}T_n\rbrace \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ such that $|\chi_x(\pi(T_i))|_{\mathcal{H}(x)} < r_i, \forall 1\leq i \leq n$. 

The interior of $X$, denoted $\mathrm{Int}(X)$ is the set of points corresponding to inner bounded homomorphisms $\chi_x : \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x)$.
<!-- end defi-14 -->
<!-- prop-8: body_md -->
\label{reduction is all of p when the point is in the interior}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean value field and $X$ be a $k$-affinoid space. Let $x \in X$ be a point of the interior $\mathrm{Int}(X)$. Then, one has $\widetilde{X_x} = \mathbb{P}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}}$
<!-- end prop-8 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
One may use Theorem 5.2 (\cite{TemkinReductionGradueeII}) or use a direct argument. Let us denote $X = \mathcal{M}(A), \chi_x : A \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x)$. By hypothesis, one has a admissible epimorphism $\pi : k\lbrace r_1^{-1}T_1, \cdots, r_n^{-1}T_n\rbrace \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$ such that $|\chi_x(\pi(T_i))|_{\mathcal{H}(x)} < r_i, \forall 1\leq i \leq n$. 

Since $\widetilde{X_x} = \mathbb{P}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}}\lbrace \widetilde{\chi_x}(\widetilde{\pi}(\widetilde{k\lbrace r_1^{-1}T_1, \cdots, r_n^{-1}T_n\rbrace})) \rbrace$, one needs to check that 
\begin{center}
$\widetilde{\chi_x}(\widetilde{\pi}(\widetilde{k\lbrace r_1^{-1}T_1, \cdots, r_n^{-1}T_n\rbrace})) = 0$. 
\end{center} 
For all $i, \widetilde{\chi_x}(\widetilde{\pi})(\widetilde{r_i^{-1}T_i}) \in \widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}_{r_i} $ and since $|\chi_x(\pi(T_i))|_{\mathcal{H}(x)} < r_i$, one gets $\widetilde{\chi_x}(\widetilde{\pi})(\widetilde{r_i^{-1}T_i}) = 0$.

Finally, $\widetilde{X_x} = \mathbb{P}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- prop-9: body_md -->
\label{elements dans tous les anneaux de valuation sont les inversibles}
Let $k$ be a graded field and $K$ a graded field over $k$. Let us recall that $\mathbb{P}_K$ is the set of all graded valuation rings $\mathcal{O}$ with $k \subset \mathcal{O}$. Given a graded valuation ring $\mathcal{O}$, one denotes by $m_\mathcal{O}$ its unique maximal ideal. 

Then, for any non-zero homogeneous element $f\in K$ such that $f \in \bigcap_{\mathcal{O} \in \mathbb{P}_K} \mathcal{O}$, then
\begin{center}
$f \in \bigcap_{\mathcal{O} \in \mathbb{P}_K} \mathcal{O}\backslash m_\mathcal{O}$ and $f^{-1} \in \bigcap_{\mathcal{O} \in \mathbb{P}_K} \mathcal{O}$.
\end{center}
<!-- end prop-9 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $x \in K$ be non-zero homogeneous element such that there exists $\mathcal{O} \in \mathbb{P}_K$ with $x\in m_\mathcal{O}$. Then $x$ is not invertible in $\mathcal{O}$. Hence, $x$ is not invertible in $A$ the subgraded ring of $K$ generated by $x$ and $k$. This implies that $x^{-1}$ is not invertible in $B$ the subgraded ring of $K$ generated by $x^{-1}$ and $k$. Let us denote $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal of $B$ containing $x^{-1}$ and $B_\mathfrak{p}$ the localization with respect to this ideal. This is a local subgraded ring of $K$ with $x^{-1}$ in its maximal ideal. By Zorn lemma, there is a maximal subring of $K$ respecting this condition. By A. Ducros (\cite{DucrosStructureCourbeAnalytique}, 2.2.40.1) this gives a valuation ring $\mathfrak{B}$ containing $k$ and $x^{-1}$ is in its maximal ideal and so, $x \notin \mathfrak{B}$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{maximum modulus}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean valued field and $X$ be a connected $k$-affinoid space such that $\mathrm{Int}(X) = X$. Let $f \in \mathcal{O}(X)$ such that there exists $x \in X$ with $|f(x)| = r = \max_{y\in X} |f(y)|$, then for all $y\in X, |f(y)| = r$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
First, if $r= 0$, then the result is clear. Let us now assume that $r>0$.

It is enough to prove it on a small neighborhood of $x$ since $X$ is connected, and so we can assume that $f$ does not vanish on $X$ and $f^{-1} \in \mathcal{O}(X)$. By proposition \ref{reduction is all of p when the point is in the interior}, one has $\widetilde{X_x} = \mathbb{P}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}}$. By lemma \ref{lemma Temkin} (lemma 4.4 of \cite{TemkinReductionGradueeII}), $\widetilde{X_x\lbrace r^{-1}f\rbrace} = \widetilde{X_x}\lbrace \tilde{f}\rbrace$ but by hypothesis $\widetilde{X_x\lbrace r^{-1}f\rbrace} = \widetilde{X_x}$ so $\tilde{f} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ is in all graded subvaluation ring of $\widetilde{\mathcal{H}(x)}$. Hence, by proposition \ref{elements dans tous les anneaux de valuation sont les inversibles}, $\tilde{f}$ is in no maximum ideal of those graded rings which implies that $\tilde{f}^{-1}$ is in all graded valuation rings. Applying lemma \ref{lemma Temkin} (4.4 of \cite{TemkinReductionGradueeII}), one gets
\begin{center}
$\widetilde{X_x\lbrace r f^{-1}\rbrace} = \widetilde{X_x}\lbrace \tilde{f}^{-1} \rbrace = \widetilde{X_x}$.
\end{center}
So, by Theorem 4.5 of \cite{TemkinReductionGradueeII} $X_x\lbrace r f^{-1}\rbrace$ and $X_x$ define the same subdomain of $X_x$. Hence, on a neighborhood $U$ of $x$, for all $y\in U, |f^{-1}(y)|\leq r$ and so $|f(y)|=r$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- rem-6: body_md -->
This result also follows from Theorem 1.5 of Gubler-Rabinoff (\cite{GublerRabinoffPSHFunctions}) which states that the local maximum principle stands for all plurisubharmonic functions on an analytic space. Since for any $f\in \mathcal{O}(X), \log |f|$ is a plurisubharmonic function, their theorem is more general result. The two results were proved independently and the two proofs differ in their construction. In their proof, they use the connectedness by curves and prove the result on curves, which by construction comes from graph theory.
<!-- end rem-6 -->
<!-- defi-15: body_md -->
Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d \geq 2$ over $\mathbb{C}$. We say that a point $x\in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ is periodic if there exists $n\in \mathbb{N}$, such that $f^{\circ n}(x) =x$. We say that $x$ is a :
\begin{itemize}
\item repelling if $|(f^{\circ n})'(x)|>1$,
\item indifferent if $|(f^{\circ n})'(x)| = 1$ and parabolic if $(f^{\circ n})'(x)$ is a root of unity,
\item attracting if $|(f^{\circ n})'(x)|<1$.
\end{itemize} 

Let us define the Fatou set $\mathcal{F}_f$ as the biggest subset of $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ on which the family $(f, f^{\circ 2}, f^{\circ 3}, \cdots)$ is normal. We define the Julia set as $J_f = \mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C}) \backslash \mathcal{F}_f$.

The Julia set can be caracterized as the following set :
\begin{center}
$\lbrace x\in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}), \forall x\in U$ open $\bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} f^{\circ n}(U)$ omits at most 2 points$\rbrace$.
\end{center}

The Julia set is also the support of the equilibrium measure, $\mu_f$, of $f$. It is the only probability measure that verifies the two following conditions :
\begin{itemize}
\item $f^*\mu = d\mu$,
\item the support of $\mu$ is disjoint from the exceptionnal set,
\end{itemize}
where the exceptionnal set is 
\begin{center}
$\mathrm{Exc}(f) := \lbrace a \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}), f^{-1}(a) = \lbrace a \rbrace \rbrace$
\end{center}
and contains at most two points.

This equilibrium measure can be obtained by taking the limit as $n \rightarrow \infty$ of the pull-backs of any Dirac measure, supported on a point not in the exceptionnal set, by $f^{\circ n}$.
<!-- end defi-15 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
Any repelling point is a point in the Julia set, any attracting point is a point in the Fatou set. Any parabolic point is in the Julia set. 

Furthermore, the repelling points are dense in the Julia set.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
Any repelling point is in the classical Julia set and any indifferent or attracting point is in the Fatou set.
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- ex-4: body_md -->
Let $k$ a complete, non-archimedean, valued field and $f(z) = z^d$ where $d\geq 2$. Then, $J_{f, classical} = \emptyset$. A reason is that in this case, all the periodic points are indifferent or attracting if the residual characteristic of $k$ divides $d$.
<!-- end ex-4 -->
<!-- defi-16: body_md -->
Any $\eta \in \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k$ extends from $k[T]$ to $k(T)$ by $ \eta (\frac{P}{Q})= \frac{\eta (P)}{\eta (Q)}$ and allowing the value $\infty$ if $\eta (Q) = 0$.

Then, any rational map $f$ over $k$ extends to a map $f : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ by 
\begin{center}
$f(\eta) := P \mapsto \eta(P\circ f)$ for all $P\in k[T]$.
\end{center}

Furthermore, for all $a\in k, f(\eta_a) = \eta_{f(a)}$. 

Finally, one can define the Berkovich Julia set as :
\begin{center}
$J_f := \lbrace x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, \forall x\in U$ open $\bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} f^{\circ n}(U)$ omits a finite number of points$\rbrace$.
\end{center}
Then, it is a compact subset of $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ and $J_f \cap\mathbb{P}^1(k) = J_{f,classical}.$

\cite{FavreRiveraLetelierBrolinEquidistribution} defined an equilibrium measure of $f, \mu_f$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ which is a probability measure supported on the Julia set, invariant by $f$.

Finally, one can consider the periodic points of $f$ in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$. We say that a point $\eta \in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is periodic if $f^n(\eta) = \eta$. If $\eta \notin \mathbb{P}^1_k$, we say that 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\eta$ is repelling if the local degree of $f^n$ at $\eta$ is $\geq 2$,
\item $\eta$ is indifferent if the local degree of $f^n$ at $\eta$ is 1.
\end{itemize}
The repelling points are in the Julia set and the type III and IV indifferent point are in the Fatou set.
<!-- end defi-16 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{Taking a field extension does not change the julia set}
Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d$ defined over a non-archimedean complete valued field $k$. Let $K$ be a field extension of $k$. Let us denote $J_k$ and $J_K$ the Julia set defined over $k$ and $K$, respectively. Let us denote $\pi : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ the projection. Then

\begin{center}
$\pi(J_K) = J_k$.
\end{center}
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Since $\pi$ is continuous and $J_K$ is compact, so is $\pi(J_K)$.

Firstly, we show that $\pi(J_K) \subset J_k$. Let $x \notin J_k$, then there exists $x \in U$ an open subset of $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ such that $\bigcup f^n(U)$ omits an infinite number of points of $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}$. Then $\bigcup f^n(\pi^{-1}(U))$ omits an infinite number of points. So, if $y \in \pi^{-1}(x)$, then $y \notin J_K$ and so $x\notin \pi(J_K)$. 

Secondly, let us denote $\mu_{f,k}$ and $\mu_{f,K}$ the equilibrium measures of $f$ seen as a rational map defined over $k$ and $K$, respectively. Then, we have $\pi_* \mu_{f,K} = \mu_{f,k}$. (We check that $f_*(\pi_* \mu_{f,K}) = \pi_* \mu_{f,K}$ and the support of $\pi_* \mu_{f,K}$ is clearly disjoint from the exceptional set which characterizes the equilibrium measure.)

So, we have $\mu_{f,k} (\pi(J_K)) = \mu_{f,K}(J_K) =1$. Since $\pi(J_K)$ is closed, it gives $J_k \subset \pi(J_K)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- rem-7: body_md -->
We will later show that if $K$ is the completion of an algebraic extension of $k$, then $\pi^{-1}(J_k) = J_K$ (proposition \ref{Taking an algebraic field extension does not change the julia set}) and if $K$ and $k$ are both algebraically closed, then there exists a continuous morphism : the canonical section, $\sigma_{K/k} : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$, such that $\sigma_{K/k}(J_k) = J_K$ (proposition \ref{Taking the Julia set over a transcendental extension does not change it}).
<!-- end rem-7 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{classical Julia set is dense}
Let $f$ be a rational map defined over a non-archimedean complete valued field $k$. If the classical Julia set $J_{f,classical}$ is non-empty, then it is dense in the Julia set $J_f$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Theorem 8.15 of Benedetto (\cite{BenedettoLivre}), if $f^{-1}(\overline{J_{f,classical}}) \subset \overline{J_{f,classical}}$, then $J_f \subset \overline{J_{f,classical}}$. So it suffices to check this condition.

Let $x \in f^{-1}(\overline{J_{f,classical}}) $ and $x \in U$ open. Since $f$ has finite fibers, $f : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is open (lemma \ref{morphisme fini sur meme dimension est ouvert}) and $f(U)$ is open. Since $f(x) \in f(U) \cap \overline{J_{f,classical}}$, there exists $y\in f(U)$ such that $y \in J_{f,classical}$. Hence, there exists $r \in U$ with $f(r) = y \in J_{f,classical}$, so $r \in J_{f,classical} \cap U$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{compact of k are compact in berkovich}
Let $k$ be a complete, algebraically closed valued field. Let $E$ be a subset of $\mathbb{P}^1(k)$. Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item $E$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{P}^1(k)$,
\item $\overline{E}^{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k} = E$ in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If $k = \mathbb{C}$, then $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k = \mathbb{P}^1(k)$ and the result is clear.

Let us now assume that $k$ is non-archimedean, then $\mathbb{P}^1(k)$ is not compact, hence we may assume that $\infty \notin E$.

$\implies$ Let us first show that $E \subset \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is compact. Let $U_i$ be an open covering of $E$ in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$. Then $U_i\cap k$ is an open covering of $E$ in $k$. So, me way find a finite subcovering which will be a covering of $E$ in $\mathbb{P}_k^{1,an}$. Hence, $E$ is compact in $\mathbb{P}_k^{1,an}$.

Since the Berkovich spaces over a field are Hausdorff, we get that $E$ is closed in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}$.

$\Longleftarrow$ Let $U_i$ be an open covering of $E$ in $k$, we may assume that all $U_i$ are open balls in $k$ : $U_i = B(a_i, r_i)$. 

By hypothesis $E$ is closed in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ so it is compact in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$. Since, $B^{an}(a_i, r_i)$ is an open covering of $E$ in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ we might find a finite covering $B^{an}(a_j, r_j)$. So, $B(a_j, r_j)$ is a finite subcovering of $E$ in $k$, so $E$ is compact in $\mathbb{P}^1(k)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean, complete, valued field and $f \in \mathrm{Rat}_d(k)$ of degree $\geq 2$. Then, the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item $J_f = J_{f, classical}$
\item $J_{f,classical}$ is a non-empty, compact in $\mathbb{P}^1(\overline{k})$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{Repelling points are dense}(Theorem 10.71, \cite{BakerRumelyBook})

Let $K$ be a non-archimedean, algebraically closed, valued field and $f$ be a rational function of degree $d \geq 2$ defined over $K$. Then, the repelling points of $f$ in $\mathbb{P}_K^{1,an}$ are dense in $J_f$.
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
(Théorème 3, \cite{BezivinPointsRepDenses})

Let $K$ be a non-archimedean, algebraically closed, valued field and $f$ be a rational function of degree $d \geq 2$ defined over $K$. If $f$ has a repelling point defined over $\mathbb{P}^1(K)$, then the repelling points are dense in the classical Julia set. Furthermore, every point of the classical Julia set is an accumulation point of repelling periodic points.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- prop-13: body_md -->
\label{repelling points of type I are dense in the Julia Set}
Let $K$ be a non-archimedean, algebraically closed, valued field and $f$ be a rational function of degree $d \geq 2$ defined over $K$. If $f$ has a repelling point defined over $\mathbb{P}^1(K)$, then the type I repelling points are dense in the Berkovich Julia set.
<!-- end prop-13 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{NumberAttractingPointsBounded}(Theorem 10.17, \cite{BenedettoLivre}) 

Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete, valued field and denote by $p$ the characteristic of its residue field. Let $f$ be a rational function of degree $d\geq 2$. Suppose $p = 0$ or $p>d$, then there can be at most $2d-2$ attracting periodic cycles.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- prop-14: body_md -->
(Proposition 5.8 \cite{RiveraLetelierEspaceHyperboliqueEtDynamique})

Let $\mathbb{C}_p$ be the completion of the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ and $f \in \mathrm{Rat}_d(\mathbb{C}_p)$ with $d\geq 2$. Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item $f$ has an indifferent periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_p}$,
\item $f$ has infinitely many indifferent periodic points in $H_{\mathbb{C}_p}$,
\item $f$ has an indifferent periodic point in $\mathbb{C}_p$,
\item $f$ has infinitely many indifferent periodic points in $\mathbb{C}_p$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-14 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{repelling in H_k implies infinitely many}(Corollaire 5.6, \cite{RiveraLetelierEspaceHyperboliqueEtDynamique})

Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ over a complete, non-archimedean valued field $k$. Then, if $f$ has a repelling periodic point in $H_k$, then $f$ has infinitely many non-repelling periodic points in $\overline{k}$, the algebraic closure of $k$.
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let us give the idea of the proof. Since $f$ has a repelling fixed point in $H_k$, it is a type II point (see for example Theorem 8.7 of \cite{BenedettoLivre}). Hence, we may assume that it is $\eta_{0,1}$ the Gauss point. The fact that it is a repelling periodic point means that $\tilde{f}$ has degree bigger or equal to 2. Hence, it has infinitely many periodic points in $\mathbb{P}^1(\overline{k})$ and infinitely many of them are not bad directions in the sense of Theorem 7.34 of \cite{BenedettoLivre}. Hence, we have infinitely many balls $D(a,1) = \lbrace x\in k, |x-a|<1\rbrace$ that satisfies $(f^n)(D(a,1)) \subset D(a,1)$ with $|a| = 1$. Since $f^n(T) \in k(T)$, we have $f^n(T) -T = \frac{P_1(T)}{P_2(T)} \in k(T)$ and $\frac{P_1}{P_2}(D(a,1)) \subset D(0,1)$. It remains true with $D^{an}(a,1) = \lbrace x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, x(T-a) <1\rbrace$. 

Since the absolute value of a rational map on the projective Berkovich line is constant outside of the convex hull of its zeros and poles, either for all $x \in D^{an}(a,1), |\frac{P_1}{P_2}(x)| = constant < 1$ or there is an $x \in D^{an}(a,1)$ such that $|\frac{P_1}{P_2}(x)|=0$ and it will be a type I point of $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$. Since $|\frac{P_1}{P_2}(\eta_{0,1})|=1$, the first case is impossible. 

So, we get a periodic point, since $f^n(B^{an}(z,1)) \subset B^{an}(z,1)$ it is non-repelling.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{2 attracting points implies infinitely many}(Lemme 6.1 + proof of the Théorème A', \cite{RiveraLetelierEspaceHyperboliqueEtDynamique})

Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ over a complete, non-archimedean valued field $k$. If $f$ has an attracting periodic point and at least an other non-repelling periodic point, then it has a repelling periodic point in $H_k$. Hence, it has infinitely many non-repelling periodic points.
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
(Théorème 3, \cite{RiveraLetelierPeriodicPointsOfRationalMaps})

Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$ over $\mathbb{C}_p$ then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item $f$ does not have any periodic point in $H_p$,
\item $f$ has finitely many non-repelling periodic points in $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}_p)$,
\item $f$ has exactly one non-repelling periodic point in $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}_p)$.

In this case, $f$ has one attracting periodic point and all the others are repelling.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{if classical julia set compact, then one attracting only}

Let $f$ be a rational map over a complete, algebraically closed, non-archimedean, valued field $\mathbb{C}_v$. Let us assume that there is subfield $K$ which is discretely valued and such that $\overline{K}$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}_v$. Furthermore, assume that $f\in K(z)$. Then, the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item The Julia set of $f$ contains only type I and type IV points,
\item $f$ has no periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$.
\end{itemize}

Futhermore in this case, $f$ has one attracting periodic point and all the others are repelling. 

In particular, the following are also equivalent : 
\begin{itemize}
\item The classical Julia set of $f$ is non-empty and compact in $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}_v)$,
\item $f$ has no periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$ and no type IV points in its Julia set.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For the first equivalence of the proposition, let us assume that the Julia set contains only type I and type IV points.  

If there is a periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$, then it cannot be in the Julia set, because it would be a type II periodic point in the Julia set (see for example Theorem 8.7 of \cite{BenedettoLivre}). So it is in a Fatou connected component $U$. But its boundary is a finite number of type II points that are periodic (see for example Theorem 9.7 of \cite{BenedettoLivre}) and in the Julia set, which is impossible.

Let us now assume that there is no periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$. Let $U$ be a connected component of the Fatou set. Then, by Theorem 11.23 of \cite{BenedettoLivre}, it cannot be a wandering component. Otherwise, it would lie in an attarcting bassin of a Type II Julia periodic point. It cannot be an indifferent component either, because the boundary is composed of type II periodic point. So it is an attracting component but it cannot be a disk, because the boundary of such an attracting component is a type II repelling periodic point so it is a domain of Cantor type. 

There can only be one, otherwise there would be at least two attracting points and so there would be a repelling periodic point in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$ by proposition \ref{2 attracting points implies infinitely many}.

So, the Julia set is the boundary of this connected component. Let us assume that there is a type II or type III point in this boundary, then we could write it $\eta_{a,r}, a\in \mathbb{C}_v$. We can assume that the attracting point is $\infty$ and $D^{an}(a,r)$ is an open set disjoint from the attracting bassin of $\infty$. Since the Julia set is of empty interior, $D^{an}(a,r)$ cannot be contained in the Julia set and so there is at least another connected Fatou component, which is impossible. Hence, there is only type I and type IV points in the Julia set.  

The second part of the proof shows that $f$ has only one attracting points and all the others are repelling.

For the second equivalence,

Let us assume that the classical Julia set of $f$ is compact and non-empty. Then, $J_{f,classical} \subset \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathbb{C}_v}$ is compact. By lemma \ref{classical Julia set is dense}, $J_f$ is the closure of the classical Julia set, hence $J_f = J_{f,classical}$. Hence, the Julia set contains only type I points, so by the first equivalence, there is no periodic points in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$ and no type IV points in the Julia sets.

Let us assume that $f$ has no periodic points in $H_{\mathbb{C}_v}$ and no type IV in its Julia set. Then, there is only type I points in the Julia set. So the Julia set is contained in $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}_v)$, so it equal to the classical set. Hence, this set is compact.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- prop-18: body_md -->
(Corollary 7.15, \cite{TruccoWanderingFatouComp})

Let $f \in K[z]$ a tame polynomial of degree $d \geq 2$, then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
\item $J_f = J_{f, classical}$,
\item All the periodic points in $K$ are repelling,
\item There is no critical periodic element in $J_p$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-18 -->
<!-- prop-19: body_md -->
\label{Taking an algebraic field extension does not change the julia set}
Let $f$ be a rational map of degree $d$ defined over a non-archimedean complete valued field $k$. Let $K$ be the completion of an algebraic field extension of $k$. Let us denote $J_k$ and $J_K$ the Julia set defined over $k$ and $K$, respectively. Let us denote $\pi : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ the projection. Then

\begin{center}
$\pi^{-1}(J_k) = J_K$.
\end{center}
<!-- end prop-19 -->
<!-- prop-20: body_md -->
\label{measure on the union of field extension has same support}
Let $(k_i)_{i\in J}$ be a family of complete valued fields and $J$ be an ordered set such that if $i\leq j$ then $k_j$ is a field extension of $k_i$. Let us denote $\pi^{j,i} : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_i}$ the projection for $i \leq j$. 

Let us assume that we have a probability measure $\mu_j$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}$ for all $j$ such that $\pi^{j,i}_*\mu_j = \mu_i$ for all $i\leq j$. Let us denote $S_j$ the support of $\mu_j$ and assume that $(\pi^{j,i})^{-1}(S_i) = S_j$.   

Let us denote $K = \widehat{\mathrm{colim}_{j\in J}k_j}$ and $\pi^j : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}$ the projection. Then one can define a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ such that for all $j\in J, \pi^j_*\mu = \mu_j$ and the support $S$ of $\mu$ satisfies $(\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j) = S$ for all $j$.
<!-- end prop-20 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let us denote $A := \lbrace F \in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K, \mathbb{R}), \exists j\in J, f\in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}, \mathbb{R}), F = f\circ \pi^j\rbrace.$ Then, by the theorem of Stone-Weierstrass (see for example the theorem 7.29 in Chapter II of \cite{HewittStrombergRealAndAbstractAnalysis}) $A$ is dense in $\mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K, \mathbb{R})$. One needs to check that if $x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$, there exists $F\in A$ such that $F(x) \neq 0$ and if $x\neq y \in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$, there exists $G\in A$ such that $G(x) \neq G(y)$. 

For the first case, since for all $x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ and for all $j \in J$, there exists $f_j \in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}, \mathbb{R})$ with $f_j(\pi^j(x)) \neq 0$ one can take any $f_j$ and consider $F = f_j \circ \pi^j$.

If $x\neq y$ there exists $P \in K[T]$ such that $|P(x)| \neq |P(y)|$. Let $\epsilon < \max(|P(x)|, |P(y)|)$, then there exists $Q \in \mathrm{colim}_{j\in J}k_j[T], ||Q-P|| <\epsilon$ and so $|Q(x)| \neq |Q(y)|$. Furthermore, $Q \in k_j[T]$ for some $j\in J$. Then $\pi^j(x) \neq \pi^j(y)$ and there exists $f_j \in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}, \mathbb{R})$ such that $f_j(\pi^j(x)) \neq f_j(\pi^j(y))$ and $F = f_j \circ \pi^j \in A$ is such that $F(x) \neq F(y)$. 

First we define $\mu$ for $F = f_j  \circ \pi^j \in A$ by 
\begin{center}
$\int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K} F d\mu = \int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}} f_j d\mu_j$.
\end{center}
One needs to check that if $f_j \circ \pi^j = g_i \circ \pi^i$ then $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}} f_j d\mu_j = \int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_i}} g_i d\mu_i$. We may assume $i \leq j$ and so $f_j \circ \pi^{j,i} = g_i$ and since $\pi^{j,i}_*\mu_j = \mu_i$ the equality stands. 

Now to define it on all $C^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K, \mathbb{R})$, one needs to check that if $F_n, G_n \in A^\mathbb{N}$ converge to the same limit, then $\int F_n d\mu = \int G_n d\mu$. But since, $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ is compact, if $F_n \rightarrow f =  \lim G_n$, then $||F_n -G_n||_\infty \rightarrow 0$ and with $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K} 1 d\mu = 1$, we get $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K} (F_n - G_n) d\mu \rightarrow 0$.

Finally, we only need to show that $S = (\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j)$ for all $j$. 

First let $j \in J$. Then, $\pi^j_*\mu = \mu_j$ and so $\pi^j(S) \subset S_j$ like in the proof on lemmma \ref{Taking a field extension does not change the julia set} and $S\subset (\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j)$.

Then, since $(\pi^{j,i})^{-1}(S_i) = S_j$ for all $i\leq j$, then $(\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j) = (\pi^i)^{-1}(S_i)$ for all $i,j$.

Let $x\in (\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j)$ for all $j$ and let $U$ be a open set of $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ containing $x$. One needs to show that there exists $f\in \mathcal{C}^0(U, \mathbb{R})$ with $\int_U fd\mu \neq 0$. It is enough to show it for a basis of neighborhood of $x$ and so we may assume that $U = \lbrace y\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K, r_1 < |P_1(y)| < s_1, \cdots, r_k < |P_k(y)| < s_k \rbrace$ with $P_l \in K[T]$. As previously, in the proof we may assume that $P_l \in \bigcup_{j\in J} k_j$ and even $P_l \in k_j$. Hence, $\pi^j(U) = V$ is open in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_j}$. Since $x\in (\pi^j)^{-1}(S_j)$ there exists $f_j \in \mathcal{C}^0(V, \mathbb{R})$ with $\int_V f_j d\mu_j \neq 0$. 

Hence, with $f = f_j \circ f_j, \int_U fd\mu \neq 0$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First let us assume that the morphism $\pi : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is finite, so $K$ is a finite algebraic extension of $k$.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               

Since $\pi(J_K) = J_k$, one has $J_K \subset \pi^{-1}(J_k)$.
Let $x\in \pi^{-1}(J_k)$ and $U$ an open subset containing $x$. Since $\pi$ is finite, $\pi(U)$ is also open and there exists $g\in \mathcal{C}^0(\pi(U), \mathbb{R})$ such that $\int_{\pi(U)} g d\mu_{f,k} \neq 0$ and so $\int_U g\circ \pi~ d\mu_{f,K} = \int_{\pi(U)} g d\mu_{f,k} \neq 0$. Hence, $x \in J_K$.

Now, let $K$ be the completion of an algebraic extension of $k$. Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal such that all the algebraic elements of $K$ over $k$ are $x_\beta$ indexed by all $\beta \leq \alpha$.

Then, we will define a tower of field extensions in the following way : 
\begin{itemize}
\item $k_0 = k$,
\item If $\beta \leq \alpha$ is the successor of an ordinal $\gamma$, then $k_\beta = k_\gamma(x_\gamma, x_\beta)$,
\item If $\beta \leq \alpha$ is a limit ordinal, then $k_\beta = \widehat{\mathrm{colim}_{\gamma <\beta}k_\gamma}$.
\end{itemize}
We will show by transfinite induction that $\forall \beta \leq \alpha, \forall \gamma \leq \beta : (\pi^{\beta, \gamma})^{-1}(J_\gamma) = J_\beta$.

For $\beta = 0$, the result is clear. 

Let $\beta$ be an ordinal such that for all $\delta<\beta$ the result is true. 

If $\beta$ is a successor ordinal $\beta = s(\delta)$, then by the beginning of the proof, $J_\beta = (\pi^{\beta, \delta})^{-1}(J_\delta)$ and the result follows for all $\gamma \leq \delta$.

If $\beta$ is a limit ordinal, then $k_\beta = \widehat{\mathrm{colim}_{\gamma <\beta}k_\gamma}$ and we are in the case of the proposition \ref{measure on the union of field extension has same support}. The only thing that we need to check is that the measure constructed in the proof is indeed the equilibrium measure of $f$ seen as a rational map over $k_\beta$. To check that $f_*\mu = \mu$, it is enough to show that for all $g\in \mathcal{C}^0(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{k_\beta}, \mathbb{R})$ with $g = g_\gamma \circ \pi^{\beta, \gamma}$ we have $\int g\circ f d\mu = \int g d\mu$. 

Which is true since 
\begin{align*}
\int g d\mu &= \int g_j \circ \pi^{\beta, \gamma} d\mu_\gamma\\
&= \int g_j \circ \pi^{\beta, \gamma} \circ f d\mu_\gamma\\
&= \int g_j \circ f \circ \pi^{\beta, \gamma} d\mu_\gamma\\
&= \int g\circ f d\mu.
\end{align*}
The equality in the second line comes from the fact that $f_*\mu_\gamma = \mu_\gamma$ and the equality in the line 3 and 4 come from the fact that $f$ commutes with the projection. 

Furthermore since the support is the inverse image of the support of $\mu_\gamma$ for all $\gamma$ it is disjoint from the exceptional set and $\mu = \mu_\beta$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- ex-5: body_md -->
Let $k = \mathbb{C}$ trivially valued and $K = \overline{\mathbb{C}(T)}$ where $\mathbb{C}(T)$ is trivially valued. Then, any $f \in \mathrm{Rat}_d(k)$ has good reduction and $J_k = \eta_{0,1}$. The map $f$ has also good reduction when we see it in $K$ and $J_K = \eta_{0,1}$ but $\pi(\eta_T) = \eta_{0,1}$ so $J_K \neq \pi^{-1}(J_k)$.
<!-- end ex-5 -->
<!-- defi-17: body_md -->
\label{definition universal point and continuous section}
Let $k$ be a complete valued field and $X$ be a $k$-analytic space. A point $x\in X$ is said to be universal if for all complete valued extension $L$ of $k$, the norm on the algebra $\mathcal{H}(x) \hat{\otimes} L$ is multiplicative. 

For $L$ a complete valued field extension of $k$, let us denote $X_L := X \hat{\otimes} L$. Then if $x \in X$ is universal it defines a canonical point $\sigma_{L/k}(x)$ which is the point corresponding to the multiplicative norm on $\mathcal{H}(x) \hat{\otimes} L$.
<!-- end defi-17 -->
<!-- prop-21: body_md -->
(Corollaire 3.14 \cite{PoineauAngelique})

If $k$ is algebraically closed, $X$ a $k$-analytic space then all points of $X$ are universal.
<!-- end prop-21 -->
<!-- ex-6: body_md -->
If $k$ is an algebraically closed, valued field, $L$ is any valued field extension, $X= \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k$ and $x\in k$. Then, $\sigma_{L/k}(x)$ is the point in $\mathbf{A}^{1,an}_L$ corresponding to the point $x$ seen as an element of $L$.

And for all $r>0$, $\sigma_{L/k}(\eta_{x,r})$ is the point $\eta_{x,r} \in \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_L$.
<!-- end ex-6 -->
<!-- prop-22: body_md -->
(Corollaire 3.7 \cite{PoineauAngelique})

Let $k$ be a complete valued field and $K$ a field extension of $k$. Let us denote $X_u$ the set of all universal points then, the map $\sigma_{K/k} : X_u \rightarrow X\hat{\otimes} K$ is continuous.

In particular, if $k$ is algebraically closed, then $\sigma_{K/k} : X \rightarrow X\hat{\otimes} K$ is continuous.
<!-- end prop-22 -->
<!-- prop-23: body_md -->
\label{Taking the Julia set over a transcendental extension does not change it}
Let $k \subset K$ with $k, K$ two complete, algebraically closed, valued fields and $f\in \mathrm{Rat}_d(k)$. Let $\sigma_{K/k} : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ the continuous section of the definition \ref{definition universal point and continuous section}.

Then, 
\begin{center}
$\sigma_{K/k}(J_k) = J_K$.
\end{center}
Hence, $J_K$ and $J_k$ are homeomorphic and $\sigma_{K/k} \circ \pi_{K/k} = \mathrm{Id}_{J_K}$.
<!-- end prop-23 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let us denote $R_k := \lbrace x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, x$ is a repelling point of type I or II$\rbrace$ and $R_K := \lbrace x\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K, x$ is a repelling point of type I or II$\rbrace$, then it suffices to show that $\sigma_{K/k}(R_k) \subset J_K$ and $R_K \subset \sigma_{K/k}(J_k)$ since $R_k$ and $R_K$ are dense in $J_k$ and $J_K$ by proposition \ref{Repelling points are dense}.

Let $x\in R_k$. If $x$ is a type I point, then $x\in k$ and $f^n(x) = x$ and $|(f^n)'(x)|>1$. Hence if we see $x$ as a point in $K$, by the correspondance $x = \sigma_{K/k}(x), x\in R_K$. So, $\sigma_{K/k}(x) \in R_K\subset J_K$.
If $x$ is a type II point, $x = \eta_{a,r}$ and there exists $M \in \mathrm{GL}_2(k)$ such that $M\cdot x = \eta_{0,1}$ and the reduction of $f^M$ is of degree at least 2. Then, all of this remains true, if we see $\eta_{a,r} \in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K,$ by the correspondance $\eta_{a,r} = \sigma(\eta_{a,r}), M\in \mathrm{GL}_2(K)$ and $\sigma_{K/k}(x) \in R_K \subset J_K$.

Let $x\in R_K$. If $x$ is a type I point, then $x\in K$ and $f^n(x) = x$ and $|(f^n)'(x)|>1$. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, $x\in k$ and $x\in \sigma_{K/k}(R_k) \subset \sigma_{K/k}(J_k)$. If $x$ is a type II point, $x = \eta_{a,r}$ then there exists $M \in \mathrm{GL}_2(K)$ such that $M\cdot x = \eta_{0,1}$ and the reduction of $f^M$ is of degree at least 2. Furthermore, if $y\in K, |y|= r$ then we may take $M$ to be 
$\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{1}{y}&\frac{-a}{y}\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}.$

Since $f^M$ has a reduction of degree $\geq 2$, then by the proof of the proposition \ref{repelling in H_k implies infinitely many}, there exists $z\in K$ such that $(f^M)^n(z) = z$ and $|z|\leq 1$. 

Then, $M^{-1}z$ is a periodic point of $f$ and so is a point of $k$. Since $M^{-1}z = yz+a$, one has $|M^{-1}z -a| = |yz| \leq r$. Hence, $\eta_{a,r} = \eta_{M^{-1}z,r}$ and $\eta_{a,r} \in \sigma_{K/k}(\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k)$. It remains to show that $\eta_{M^{-1}z,r} \in J_k$. Since $\eta_{M^{-1}z,r} = \pi(\eta_{a,r}) \in \pi(J_K)$, we have that $\eta_{M^{-1}z,r} \in J_k$ by lemma \ref{Taking a field extension does not change the julia set}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{Taking the Julia set over any extension does not change it}
Let $k$ be a complete valued field, $K$ be a complete valued field extension. Then, $\widehat{\overline{K}}$ the completion of an algebraic closure of $K$ is a valued field extension of $\widehat{\overline{k}}$. Let us denote $\pi_{K, k}, \pi_{\widehat{\overline{k}}, k}, \pi_{\widehat{\overline{K}}, K}$ the projections and $\sigma_{\widehat{\overline{K}}, \widehat{\overline{k}}}$ the continuous section. 

Then,
\begin{center}
$\pi_{K,k}(J_K) = J_k$ and $\pi_{\widehat{\overline{K}}, K}\circ \sigma_{\widehat{\overline{K}}, \widehat{\overline{k}}}~ (\pi_{\widehat{\overline{k}}, k}^{-1}(J_k)) = J_K$.
\end{center}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- defi-18: body_md -->
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete value field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space. An analytic family of rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$, parametrized by $X$, is an analytic map $f : X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k \rightarrow X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ such that $\mathrm{pr}_X = \mathrm{pr}_X \circ f$ where $\mathrm{pr}_X : X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is the first projection and for all $x \in X, f_x := f(x, \cdot) : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ is a rational map of degree $d\geq 2$.

A pair $(x,z) \in X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ can be seen as an element $x\in X$ and $z\in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ and this will be the point of view used in the rest of this article.
<!-- end defi-18 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a complete algebraically closed non-archimedean field, let $U \subset \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_K$ be a connected set, and let $(f_\lambda)_{\lambda \in U}$ be an analytic family of rational maps. Assume that the type I repelling points are dense in $J_{x_0}$ for some $x_0 \in U$. Then, the following are equivalent :
\begin{enumerate}
\item The Julia sets move analytically on $U$,
\item For all $x\in U, f_x$ has no unstably indifferent periodic point and no type I repelling periodic points with multiplicity greater than 1.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- defi-19: body_md -->
Let $f$ be an analytic map and $x\in X$. We say that the Julia moves continuously on a neighborhood of $x$ if there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that for all $y\in U$ and all family $(y_i)_{i\in I} \in U^I$ with $y$ in the closure of the $(y_i)$, we have :
\begin{center}
$\overline{\lbrace (f, z) \in X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, \exists i\in I, y_i = f~and~z \in J_f\rbrace} \cap \mathrm{pr}_X^{-1}(y) = \lbrace (f, z) \in X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, f=y$ and $z \in J_y\rbrace$
\end{center}
where $\overline{E}$ denotes the closure of the set $E$.

This means that one requires
\begin{center}
$\overline{\bigcup J_{y_i}} \cap \mathrm{pr}^{-1}_X(y) = J_y$
\end{center}
where we see the Julia set $J_z$ embedded in $X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ in the fiber $\mathrm{pr}^{-1}_X(z)$.
<!-- end defi-19 -->
<!-- rem-8: body_md -->
In the case, where the field $k$ is countable $X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k$ is metrizable and this definition is equivalent to the continuity of the family of compact sets $(\lbrace (x, y), y\in J_x\rbrace)_{x \in X}$ with respect to the Haussdorf distance.
<!-- end rem-8 -->
<!-- defi-20: body_md -->
\label{Definition of the periodic point}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps of degree $d \geq 2$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Let $U$ be a small enough open of $X$ such that for all $x\in X, f_x =\frac{a_d(x)z^d+ \cdots + a_0(x)}{b_d(x)z^d+ \cdots +b_0(x)}$ and all the $a_i$ and $b_i$ are in $\mathcal{O}(U)$. Let $V$ be an open set of $X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}$ such that $\mathrm{pr}_X(V) \subset U$, then $f_x^n(z)-z = \frac{P_1(z)}{P_2(z)} \in \mathcal{O}(V)$. Hence, one can define $C^n_V := \lbrace (x,z) \in V, |f_x^n(z)-z|=0 \rbrace$ the closed analytic space of the fixed points of $f^n$. For each $(x,z)\in C^n_V, z$ can be seen as type I points in $\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$.
<!-- end defi-20 -->
<!-- prop-24: body_md -->
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps of degree $d \geq 2$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Let $C^n_V$ be as in definition \ref{Definition of the periodic point}, then 
\begin{center}
If $x\in \mathrm{Int} (X)$, then for all $(x,t) \in \mathrm{pr}_X^{-1}(x), (x,t) \in \mathrm{Int} (C^n_V)$
\end{center}
where $\mathrm{pr}_X$ is the projection from $C^n_V$ to $X$ via the first coordinate.
<!-- end prop-24 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By the third point of the proposition 2.5.8 of \cite{BerkovichLivre}, one only needs to check that $(x,t) \in \mathrm{Int} (C^n_V/X)$.

Since this map has finite fibers, it is locally finite (lemme \ref{morphisme fini sur meme dimension est ouvert}). So, by the converse implication of the Corollary 2.5.13 of \cite{BerkovichLivre}, $(x,t) \in \mathrm{Int} (C^n_V/X)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- defi-21: body_md -->
A $k$-analytic space will be said without boundary if $\mathrm{Int} (X) = X$.
<!-- end defi-21 -->
<!-- defi-22: body_md -->
\label{Definition of persistently indifferent}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps and $x \in X$. A periodic point $z \in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ of $f_x$ of period $n$ of type I is said to be persistently indifferent if :
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
\begin{center}
    There is a neighborhood $U$ of $(x,z)$ such that $\forall (\lambda, y) \in U$ if $y$ is a type I periodic point of $f_\lambda$ of period $n$, then $|(f_\lambda^n)'(y)| =1$. 
\end{center}
<!-- end defi-22 -->
<!-- rem-9: body_md -->
There is a difference with the archimedean case here. Since the indifferent point can be in the algebraic closure of the residual field of $f_\lambda$, they can have a multiplier strictly greater than 1.
So, we cannot necessarily have an analytic motion of the indifferent point, hence we have a result on a neighborhood of the point instead of following holomorphically the point on a neighborhood.
<!-- end rem-9 -->
<!-- ex-7: body_md -->
Let us assume that $k$ is algebraically closed and $f\in \mathrm{Rat}_d(k)$. Then all indifferent periodic point of $f$ are persistently indifferent.

Let $(f,z) \in (\mathrm{Rat}_d \times \mathbb{P}^1)^{an}(k)$ be an indifferent point. Then, $(f^n)'(z)  \in k$, hence $U = \lbrace (y,t) \in (\mathrm{Rat}_d\times \mathbb{P}^1)^{an}, |(f^n_y)'(t) - (f^n)'(z)|<1\rbrace$ is a neighborhood of $(f,z)$. This implies that if $(y,t)$ is a periodic point of $f_y$ of period $n$, then it is indifferent. So $z$ is persistently indifferent.
<!-- end ex-7 -->
<!-- defi-23: body_md -->
Let $K$ be algebraically closed, complete, valued field and $X \subset \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_K$.
Let us recall the definition of unstably indifferent in the sens of Silverman \cite{TSilvermanNonArchiLambdaLemma}. Let $f : X \times_K \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K\rightarrow X\times_K\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ be an analytical family of map of degree $d$. Then, for all $x\in X, f_x : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ is a rational map of degree $d$. So, one can see $f'_\lambda : \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(x)}$ as a rational map of degree $e$. And so one get $f' : X\times_K \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K \rightarrow X\times_K \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$ an analytical family of rational map. Let $(x,t)$ be an indifferent periodic point. By replacing $f$ by some $f^{\circ n}$, we may suppose that it is of period 1. 

Then it is unstably indifferent if $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K}(f'(x,t)) = \eta_{0,1}$.
<!-- end defi-23 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{Unstably and not persistently indifferent is the same in dimension one}
Let $K$ be algebraically closed, complete, valued field and $X \subset \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_K$. Then a point $(x,t)$ is not persistently indifferent if and only if $(x,t)$ is unstably indifferent in the sense of Silverman.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $(x,t)$ be a periodic point, then we may find an open neighborhood such that $C_V$ is well defined (see definition \ref{Definition of the periodic point}). Then, we can consider $g = \mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}}\circ f' : C_V \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$.

Let us assume that $g(x,t) = \eta_{0,1}$, then by the Corollaire 3.5.7 of Ducros \cite{DucrosStructureCourbeAnalytique} the fiber $g^{-1}(\eta_{0,1})$ has dimension $0$. Hence, the morphism is quasi-finite on $(x,t)$, so it is open (lemma \ref{morphisme fini sur meme dimension est ouvert}). So, $g(C_V)$ is an open that contains $g(x,t) = \eta_{0,1}$, so for all neighborhood $V$ of $(x,t)$, there exists $(y,z) \in V$ such that $|(f_y)'(z)| > 1$ and $f_y(z) = z$ and $(x,t)$ is not persistently indifferent.

Let us assume that $g(x,t) \neq \eta_{0,1}$, then there exists $U$ a neighborhood of $g(x,t)$ such that $U \subset \overline{D^{an}(0,1)} \backslash D^{an}(0,1)$ and the open $g^{-1}(U)$ is a neighborhood of $(x,t)$ wich makes $(x,t)$ persistently indifferent.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{Unstably and not persistently indifferent is the same}
Let $K$ be algebraically closed, complete, valued field and $X$ be a $K$-analytic space. Then, for any point $(x,t) \in X\times_K \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_K$, 
\begin{center}
$(x,t)$ is persistently indifferent if and only if $g(x,t) \neq \eta_{0,1}$
\end{center}
where $g$ is defined in the lemma \ref{Unstably and not persistently indifferent is the same in dimension one}.
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
As in lemma \ref{Unstably and not persistently indifferent is the same in dimension one}, if $g(x,t)\neq \eta_{0,1}, (x,t)$ is persistently indifferent.

Assume that $g(x,t) = \eta_{0,1}$ and let $U$ be a neighborhood of $(x,t)$ in $C_V$. By the Corollaire 3.5.7 of Ducros \cite{DucrosStructureCourbeAnalytique} the fiber $g^{-1}(\eta_{0,1})$ is of dimension strictly smaller than the dimension of $U$, hence there exists $\eta_{a,r} \neq \eta_{0,1} \in g(U)$. 

If $\max(|a|, r) >1$, then $(x,t)$ is not persistently indifferent through $U$ and we are done. Let us now assume the contrary, hence $|a|\leq 1$ and $r<1$. So there exists $(y,z)\in U$ such that $|g(y,z)(T-a)| = r<1$ and so $g^*(T-a) \in \mathcal{O}(U)$ is not constant in 	absolute value. So by the theorem \ref{maximum modulus}, there exists $(l, w) \in U$ with $|g(l,w)(T-a)|>1$ and since $|a|\leq 1, |g(l,w)(T)|>1$. Hence, $(x,t)$ is not persistently indifferent through $U$, so it is not persistently indifferent.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{JuliaSetMovesContinuouslyNonArchi}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space with no boundary. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps and $x \in X$. Let us assume that $f_x$ has type I repelling points. Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{itemize}
    \item The Julia set moves continously on a neighborhood of $x$, 
    \item There exists $U \subset X$ open with $x\in U$ such that for all $y\in U$, every point of $f_y$ is attracting, repelling or persistently indifferent. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The proof is based on the presentation by McMullen (\cite{McMullenComplexDynamicsAndRenormalization}) of Mané-Sad-Sullivan's theorem.
    
    $\implies$ Let us assume that the Julia set depends continously on $\lambda$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $x$.
    Let $y\in U$ and let $z \in \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_{\mathcal{H}(y)}$ be an indifferent type I point of period $n$. 
    
   Since $z \notin J_y$ and the Julia sets moves continuously, one can find a neighborhhod $V$ of $(y,z)$ such that for all $(w, t) \in V, t \notin J_w$. Let us now consider the closed analytic space $C^n_V$ where $C_V^n$ is defined in \ref{Definition of the periodic point}. We may restrict $U$ such that $(y,z) \in C^n_V$ and for all $(w,t) \in C^n_V, |(f^n_w)'(t)|\leq 1$. So we can apply theorem \ref{maximum modulus} to see that for all $(w,t) \in C^n_V, |(f^n_w)'(t)| = 1$ and $z$ is a persistent indifferent point.
   
   $\Longleftarrow$ Let us assume that for all $y$ sufficiently close to $x$, every point of $f_y$ is attracting, repelling or persistently indifferent. Then we claim that there exists a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ such that each cycle of repelling, indifferent, attracting points remain repelling, indifferent, attracting throughout $V$. 
   
  Let $U$ be the neighborhood of $x$ where the hypothesis is verified. We may restrain $U$ such that $f_x= \frac{a_d(x)z^d+ \cdots + a_0(x)}{b_d(x)z^d+ \cdots + b_0(x)}$ with $a_i(x), b_i(x) \in \mathcal{O}(U)$. And we may assume that for all $y \in U, \infty_y \notin J_y$. Let $\mathcal{U} = U\times_k \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k$ and let $n \geq 1$. We claim that on each connected component of $C^n_\mathcal{U}$ all the periodic cycle remain repelling, indifferent or attracting.
  
Let $C$ be a connected component of $C^n_\mathcal{U}$ and $(y,t) \in C$. There is a neighborhhod $U_{y,t}$ of $(y,t)$ in $C$ such that the periodic points remain repelling, indifferent or attracting. Since $C = \bigcup_{(y,t)\in C} U_{y,t}$ they remain repelling, indifferent or attracting througout the connected component. 
	   
  Hence $V = U$ satisfies what we want.   
   
   \bigskip
   Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $x$ such that forall $y \in U, f_y$ has type I repelling points. It exists since $f_x$ has at least one type I repelling point and it is an open condition. We may suppose that throughout $U$ each cycle of attracting, repelling or indifferent remain attracting, repelling or indifferent .  
   
Let $(x_i)_{i\in I} \in U^I$ be a family of points with $x$ in the closure of this family. Let us denote $(x, J_x) := \lbrace (x,z) | z \in J_x\rbrace$ and $L_x := \overline{\lbrace (y, z) \in X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, \exists i\in I, x_i = y~\mathrm{and}~z \in J_y\rbrace} \cap \mathrm{pr}^{-1}_X(x)$. 
   
   To show that $(x,J_x) \subset L_x$, it suffices to show that $R_x = \lbrace (x,z) | z$ is a repelling point of $f_x\rbrace \subset L_x$. Let $z$ be a repelling point of $f_x$. Since the points remain repelling in the connected component of $C^n_{U\times_k\mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k}$ we may find $(x_i, z_i)$ with $z_i$ a repelling point and $(x_i, z_i) \rightarrow (x,z)$. Hence, $(x,z) \in L_x$. Then, $R_x \subset L_x$.
   
   Let us now show that $L_x \subset J_x$. Since the repelling, indifferent, attracting points remain repelling, indifferent, attracting throughout $U$, every family $(x_i, z_i)$ with $z_i$ a repelling point of $f_{x_i}$ gives a repelling point $z_i^{f_{x_i}}$ of $f_x$ of the same period. It is a point of the connected component of $C^n_\mathcal{U}$ in $\mathrm{pr}^{-1}_X(x)$. 
   
   Since $L_x =  \overline{\lbrace (y, z) \in X\times_k \mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k, \exists i\in I, x_i = y~\mathrm{and}~z~\mathrm{is~repelling} \rbrace} \cap \mathrm{pr}^{-1}_X(x)$, it is enough to verify that if $(x_i, z_i) \rightarrow (x, z)$ with $z_i$ a repelling point of $f_{x_i}$, then $z \in J_x$. For $i$ big enough, each $(x_i, z_i) \in U$ and so it gives a repelling point $z_i^{f_{x_i}}$ of $f_x$. It suffices to verify that $(x,z)$ is a cluster point of $(x, z_i^{f_{x_i}})$.  
   
   Assume that it is not true, then there exists an open $V$ of $(x,z)$ such that for all big enough $i, (x, z_i^{f_{x_i}}) \notin V$. We might reduce $V$ such that there exists $V'$ open with $V \cap V' = \emptyset$ and all $(x, z_i^{f_{x_i}})$ are in $V'$. Then all $(x_i, z_i)$ are in $V'$ for $i$ big enough witch is a contradiction to the fact that $(x_i, z_i) \rightarrow (x, z)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- prop-25: body_md -->
\label{JuliaSetsMovesContinuouslyIfAttractingBounded}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean complete valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space with no boundary. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps of degree $d \geq 2$. Let $x\in X$ such that $f_x$ has type I repelling points. 

Furthermore, let us assume that $f_x$ has a finite number of attracting points.

Then the following are equivalent :
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The Julia set depends continously on $\lambda$ on a neighborhood of $x$, 
    \item The number of attracting cycles is constant on a neighborhood of $x$,
    \item The maximum period of an attracting cycle of $f_\lambda$ is locally bounded at $x$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-25 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
$ 1 \implies 2$ By theorem \ref{JuliaSetMovesContinuouslyNonArchi}, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that the attracting, indifferent and repelling cycle periodic remain attracting, indifferent and repelling cycle periodic throughout $U$. Since $f_x$ has a finite number of attracting points, the number of attracting cycles is constant on a neighborhood.

$2 \implies 3$ Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $x$ such that for all $y\in U$, $f_y$ has $l$ attracting cycles. Since each attracting cycle of $x$ gives an attracting cycle of $y$, with period smaller or equal, for $y$ close enough to $x$. So, on a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ the maximum period of an attracting cycle is bounded on $V$. 

$3 \implies 1$ Let us assume that it is bounded by $N-1$. Let $n \geq N, y \in V$ and $(y,t)$ an indifferent periodic point of $f_y$ of period $n$. It suffices to show that $(y,t)$ is persistently indifferent. Let $\mathcal{V}$ a neighborhood of $(y,t)$ and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the connected component of $C^n_\mathcal{V}$ that contains $(y,t)$. Since there is no attracting cycle of period $n$ in $V$, the cycle remains indifferent on $C$, otherwise it would be a contradiction with the theorem \ref{maximum modulus} applied to $((f^{\circ n})')^{-1}$. So, $(y,t)$ is persistently indifferent. 

Let now $n$  be smaller than $N$ and $(y,t)$ an indifferent periodic point of period $n$. If $(y,t)$ is not persistently indifferent, then on any neighborhood of $(y,t)$ they are attracting or repelling point of period dividing $n$. If there was only attracting and indifferent points of period dividing $n$ in one of the neighborhood, it would be a contradiction with the maximum modulus principle (see theorem \ref{maximum modulus}).

Let us assume by contradiction that there exists $(y_i, t_i)$ repelling point of period dividing $n$ with $(y_i, t_i) \rightarrow (y,t)$. Since the Julia set is perfect (see for exemple \cite{BenedettoLivre}, Theorem 8.15), and the repelling points of type I are dense in the Julia set if they exist, which is the case here, there exists $(y_i, t_i^j) \rightarrow (y_i, t_i)$ for all $i$, with $(y_i, t_i^j)$ repelling points of period $l_i^j \geq N$. Since, the repelling points of period $\geq N$ remain repelling, for all $j, (y_i, t_i^j)$ gives a repelling point $(y,t^j)$ and $(y,t)$ will be a cluster point of $(y,t^j)$. Hence, $(y,t) \in J_y$ and it is a repelling point, which is a contradiction. 

So, $(y,t)$ is peristently indifferent.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- rem-10: body_md -->
By theorem \ref{NumberAttractingPointsBounded}, if the residual characteristic of $k$ is $0$ or is strictly smaller than the degree $d$ of the family of rational maps, then for all $x\in X, f_x$ has a finite number of attracting points $(\leq 2d-2)$ and the proposition \ref{JuliaSetsMovesContinuouslyIfAttractingBounded} applies.
<!-- end rem-10 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{z^2+ T has only repelling points}
Let us consider $k$ a non-archimedean, complete, algebraically closed, field with residue characteristic $\neq 2$. Let us denote $X = \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k \backslash \overline{D^{an}(0,1)}$. Let $f : X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1, an}_k \rightarrow X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1, an}_k$ be the analytic family of rational maps of degree $2$ such that for all $x\in X, f_x : z \mapsto z^2 + T(x)$, where $T(x)$ denotes the image of $T$ the coordinate of $\mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k$ in the residual field $\mathcal{H}(x)$. 
Then, the Julia sets moves continuously on $X$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $z$ be a periodic point of $f_x$ in the algebraic closure of $\mathcal{H}(f_x)$. Then, it is enough to show that $z$ is not an indifferent point. 

First, let us show that if there exists $d\geq 1$ with $f^d(z) = z$, then $|z| = \sqrt{|T(x)|}$. 

One has that $f^{\circ d}(y)$ is a polynomial in $y$ with $f^{\circ d}(y) = y^{2^d} + a_{2^d -2}y^{2^d -2} + a_{2^d -4}y^{2^d -4} + \cdots + a_0$ where $a_{2k}$ is a polynomial in $T(x)$ with integers coefficient and $|a_{2k}|= |T(x)|^{2^{d-1} - k}$.

And necessarily $|z| = \sqrt{|T(x)|}$.

Furthermore $(f^{\circ d})' = ((f^{\circ d-1})^2 + T(x))' = 2 f^{\circ d-1} (f^{\circ d-1})'$. 

By induction, $(f^{\circ d})' = 2^d f^{\circ d-1}f^{\circ d-2}\cdots f\times \mathrm{Id}$. So $(f^{\circ d})'(z) = 2^d z f(z) \cdots f^{\circ d-1}(z)$ and all $z, f(z), \cdots, f^{\circ d-1}(z)$ are periodic points, so they all have absolute value $\sqrt{|T(x)|}> 1$. Hence, 
\begin{center}
$|(f^{\circ d})'(z)|>1$.
\end{center}

So all periodic points are repelling, except $\infty$ which is an attracting periodic point. Therefore, we can use lemma \ref{If f has no indifferent point, then Julia sets moves continuously} to conclude.

However the continuity does not extend to the point $\eta_{0,1} \in \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_k$. Indeed, the Julia set of $f_{\eta_{0,1}}$ is only one point.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{Tz^3 + Z^2 moves continuously}
Let us consider $\mathbb{C}$ trivially valued and let $X = D^{an}(0,1)\backslash \lbrace 0 \rbrace$. So $X = \lbrace \eta_{0,r}, 0<r<1\rbrace$. Let $f : X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1, an}_k \rightarrow X \times_k \mathbb{P}^{1, an}_k$ be the analytic family of rational maps of degree $3$ such that for all $x\in X, f_x : z \mapsto T(x)z^3 + z^2$. 

Then, the Julia sets moves continuously on $X$.
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
First, since $\tilde{f_x} = z^2$, $f_x$ has $\eta_{0,1}$ as a type II repelling point, hence it has infinitely many non-repelling points. The fixed point of $f_x$ are $\lbrace 0, \infty, \frac{-1 + \alpha}{2T}, \frac{-1 - \alpha}{2T}\rbrace$ with $\alpha \in \mathcal{H}(f_x)$ such that $\alpha^2 = 1+ 4T(x)$. Hence, one of $\frac{-1 + \alpha}{2T(x)}, \frac{-1 - \alpha}{2T(x)}$ has absolute value $\frac{1}{|2T(x)|}>1$, and $f'_T( \frac{-1 \pm \alpha}{2T(x)}) = 3 - \frac{-1 \pm \alpha}{2T(x)}$ and so for one of them $|f'_x( \frac{-1 \pm \alpha}{2T(x)})| >1$ and $f_x$ has type I repelling points.

Since $X \subset \mathbf{A}^{1,an}_\mathbb{C}$, we will only need to show that no periodic points are unstably periodic, by the lemma \ref{Unstably and not persistently indifferent is the same}. 

Let us assume that $(x,t)$ is an unstably periodic point so $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathbb{P}^{1,an}_k} \circ f'(x,t) = \eta_{0,1}$. So we have a morphism of valued field $\mathcal{H}(\eta_{0,1}) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x,t)$. Let us write $x = \eta_{0,r}$, with $0 < r < 1$, then $\mathcal{H}(x) = \mathbb{C}((T))$ where $|T| = r$. The field $\mathcal{H}(x,t)$ is an algebraic extension of $\mathcal{H}(x)$ and so it can be isometrically embedded in $\bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}^*} \mathbb{C}((T^{\frac{1}{n}}))$. But $\mathcal{H}(\eta_{0,1}) = \mathbb{C}(T_2)$ with $|T_2|=1$, so we can't get a valued morphism $\mathcal{H}(\eta_{0,1}) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(x,t)$. Otherwise, $T_2$ would be send to a element of $\mathcal{H}(x,t)$ of absolute value 1. So, it is of the form $a + \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}} a_\alpha T^\alpha,$ with $a, a_\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$. Then, $T_2 -a$ is send to an element of norm $<1$ and $|T_2 -a| =1$.  

Hence, $(x,t)$ is not unstably periodic. So the Julia set moves continuously.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{If f has no indifferent point, then Julia sets moves continuously}
Let $k$ be a non-archimedean, complete, valued field and $X$ a $k$-analytic space. Let $f$ be an analytic family of rational maps of degree $d\geq 2$. Let assume that $char(\tilde{k}) = 0$ or $char(\tilde{k}) = p>d$. Let $x \in X$ such that $f_x$ has repelling points and assume that $f_x$ has a finite number of indifferents point and all of them are persistently indifferent.
